sections.h2: How do you record a deed in Lake County, Ohio, step by step?
sections.html:
A Lake County deed makes two stops in Painesville. First it goes to the Transfer Office in the Auditor's office on the first floor, where you sign an Exempt Form or a Conveyance Fee Form. Then it goes to the Lake County Recorder on the lower level of the Administration Building, who records it and, in person, returns it while you wait.

The recorder's contact page gives 105 Main Street, Lower Level, P.O. Box 490, Painesville, OH 44077, phone (440) 350-2510 and recorder@lakecountyohio.gov, with hours of 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Monday through Friday except holidays. The fee page says the last daily recordings are taken before 3:45 p.m., so plan the trip around that cutoff.

Mail works too, with conditions. Every auditor and engineer stamp must already be on the deed, you enclose a cover letter, separate checks for the recorder and the auditor, and a self-addressed stamped envelope. A deed without the auditor's stamp is rejected and sent back.

sections.h2: What does recording a deed cost in Lake County?
sections.html:
The recorder's guidelines put most documents at $34.00 for the first two pages plus a $5.00 preservation fee, for $39.00 in all, and $8.00 for each added page. The auditor collects the transfer charges separately, which is why the office asks for two checks.

Lake County deed charges listed on the recorder's guidelines and record-a-deed pages and on the auditor's transfer page

The Auditor's Real Estate FAQ explains the $4.00 as two layers: the state share of $1.00 per $1,000 and a county share of $3.00 per $1,000 that the county commissioners adopted by resolution on March 26, 1990, under section 322.02.

sections.h2: What does the Lake County Auditor need before a transfer?
sections.html:
The Auditor's Real Estate FAQ answers the questions sellers ask most. The grantor, the grantee or a representative can bring the deed in, and the office accepts transfers by mail. Whoever files must have the paperwork complete, signed and notarized, and the Transfer Office takes deeds from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

  • Every transfer needs either a DTE 100 or a DTE 100EX.
  • A parcel on homestead or the CAUV farm program also needs a notarized DTE 101 or DTE 102 before the transfer is submitted.
  • Any sale that is not a full sublot in a platted subdivision, such as part of a sublot or a metes and bounds description, must be reviewed by the Tax Map Department. Exempt transfers skip that review.
  • To remove a person from a deed, a new deed has to be created. The FAQ suggests a title company or a lawyer.

The office shows owner names exactly as they appear on the recorded deed, so a spelling slip on the deed carries straight into the county's records.

sections.h2: Which Lake County transfers skip the conveyance fee?
sections.html:
Section 319.54(G)(3) of the Revised Code lists exemptions, and the filer writes the reason on the exemption statement under section 319.202. A few that matter to a house seller:

  • A deed made only to give or release security for a debt.
  • A sale for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • A transfer between persons under the survivorship provisions of sections 5302.17 or 5302.18.
  • A transfer to a trustee when the grantor kept an unlimited power to revoke the trust.
  • A transfer to a buyer who is not a dealer and takes title only as a step in a prompt resale.

The Recorder's page adds a practical note: a Transfer on Death Beneficiary Designation Affidavit does not go through the Auditor's office and can be mailed straight to the recorder with the recording fee and a return envelope.

sections.h2: Can you record a Lake County deed electronically?
sections.html:
Yes. The recorder's Record A Deed page says a deed can now be e-recorded and lists four partner companies: Corporation Service Company, eRecording Partners Network, Simplifile and Hop Docs. You contact one of them directly, since the office does not run the portal itself.

The recorder's e-recording page also points to two search tools for records: the AVA search engine for basic information and Laredo Select for advanced searching, which asks you to register an account. The page adds that watermarks are not accepted in filings. The recorder also runs a property fraud alert service, listed among the office's services.

sections.h2: What is Lake County like, and why does that matter for a sale?
sections.html:
Lake County sits on the southern shore of Lake Erie and belongs to the Cleveland metropolitan area, with Painesville as the county seat and Mentor as the largest city. It was created on March 6, 1840, from Cuyahoga and Geauga land. Its total area is 979 square miles, but only 227 of them are land, which makes it Ohio's smallest county by land area. The shoreline runs 31 miles. Old glacial lake beaches show up as ridges, and roads such as South Ridge and Lake Shore Boulevard follow them.

Census QuickFacts counts 232,217 residents for July 2025 and 107,571 housing units, with about 1,014 people per square mile. The owner-occupied rate is 75.8 percent, the median owner-occupied home is valued at $214,100, median gross rent is $1,113 and median household income is $80,925. Interstate 90 and State Route 2 run along the county, with State Route 44 connecting them, and Laketran runs buses to downtown Cleveland.

School district names on a listing help buyers: Mentor Public Schools, Painesville City Local, Willoughby-Eastlake City, Wickliffe City, Kirtland Local, Madison Local, Perry Local, Riverside Local and Fairport Harbor Exempted Village all serve parts of the county. Lake Erie College in Painesville and Lakeland Community College in Kirtland are the county's colleges.

sections.h2: What formatting does the Lake County Recorder expect on a deed?
sections.html:
The recorder's guidelines repeat the layout rules from section 317.114, and the office will accept a deed that misses them while charging the $20.00 penalty in the table. Use this as a checklist before you sign:

  • Font size of at least 10 point on paper between 8.5 by 11 and 8.5 by 14 inches.
  • Black or blue ink only, with no highlighting.
  • Margins of 1 inch on each side and at the bottom.
  • A 3 inch margin at the top of page one for the auditor and recorder stamps, and 1.5 inches on the remaining pages.
  • The title, date, typed names under signatures, a complete notary block with commission expiration, and a full legal description.
  • The name of the preparer on the document.

The guidelines add that a later document referencing an earlier one should cite the document number or the book and page with the recording date, and each such reference costs $4.00.

faqs.q: Where is the Lake County Recorder's office?
faqs.a: It is at 105 Main Street, Lower Level, in Painesville, Ohio 44077, with a P.O. Box 490 mailing address. The phone number on the contact page is (440) 350-2510. The office is open 8:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Monday through Friday except holidays.

faqs.q: How much is the Lake County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The Auditor's Real Estate FAQ states $4.00 for every $1,000 of the purchase price, plus a $0.50 transfer fee for each parcel. The fee is paid to the Auditor before the recorder sees the deed.

faqs.q: Do I need two checks to record a deed in Lake County?
faqs.a: Yes. The recording guidelines ask for separate checks for each office, one payable to the Lake County Recorder and one to the Lake County Auditor for the transfer fees. Mail filings also need a self-addressed stamped envelope, or the document is returned collect on delivery.

faqs.q: Does a Lake County deed need the Tax Map review?
faqs.a: It does when there is consideration and the property is not a full sublot in a platted subdivision. That covers part of a sublot and metes and bounds descriptions. Exempt transfers do not need the review.

faqs.q: Can I mail a deed to the Lake County Auditor?
faqs.a: Yes, the Auditor's FAQ says transfers by mail are accepted. The Recorder's page gives the mailing address as the Auditor's Real Estate Transfer Office, 105 Main Street, PO Box 490, Painesville, OH 44077, and the office passes a transferred deed to the recorder.
